14000: "Run in" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together create a new meaning). It is also used as a noun ("a run-in"). The tricky thing about it is that it has several different meanings depending on the context — but each one is very learnable once you see them clearly.
Meaning 1: A conflict or confrontation (Noun — most common usage)

This is by far the most common meaning you will encounter in everyday English.

A run-in (always hyphenated when used as a noun) means an argument, disagreement, or unpleasant encounter with someone. It suggests a clash — two people or forces bumping against each other.

Examples:

  • "She had a run-in with her manager over the deadline."
  • "He got into trouble after a run-in with a local gang."
  • "I had a run-in with my landlord about the broken heater."

Notice the typical pattern: have a run-in with someone. The word "with" almost always follows it.

This meaning carries a slightly negative tone — a run-in is rarely pleasant. It suggests the encounter was tense, hostile, or at least uncomfortable.

A special sub-use — run-in with the law:
You will very often see this phrase specifically used for trouble with authority, especially the police:

  • "He had several run-ins with the law in his youth."
  • "Her first run-in with the police happened when she was just seventeen."

Here, "the law" is a common informal way of referring to police or the legal system.
Meaning 2: To arrest someone (Phrasal verb — informal, mainly British)

When used as a verb — to run someone in — it means for the police to arrest a person and take them to the station.

Examples:

  • "The officer ran him in for causing a disturbance."
  • "They were run in for questioning after the robbery."

The structure is: run + [person] + in or run in + [person].

This is considered informal and is more common in British English than American English. An American speaker would more likely say "take someone in" or "arrest someone." But you will come across this in British novels, films, and news.
Meaning 3: To break in a new engine (Phrasal verb — mainly British)

This is a technical but very common meaning in the context of vehicles and machines.

When you buy a brand-new car, motorcycle, or engine, you are advised not to push it to full speed or power immediately. You drive it gently for the first several hundred miles so the mechanical parts can settle into each other properly. This careful initial period is called running in (or in American English, breaking in).

Examples:

  • "I just bought a new motorcycle, so I'm still running it in."
  • "The manual says to avoid high speeds while running in the engine."
  • "This car has been run in carefully — it's never been pushed hard."

You may also see the noun form: the run-in period or the running-in period, meaning the initial careful-use phase of a machine.

This meaning is predominantly British English. Americans typically say "break in" for the same idea:

  • British: "running in a new car"
  • American: "breaking in a new car"
Meaning 4: To go into a place quickly or briefly (Phrasal verb)

This is the most literal use of "run in." It simply means to enter a place quickly or for a short time, often as a quick errand.

Examples:

  • "I'll just run in and grab my wallet — be right back."
  • "She ran in to pick up the parcel and came back out in two minutes."
  • "Can you run in to the shop and get some milk?"

Here, "run" doesn't literally mean to sprint. It just implies doing something quickly and without staying long. It's a casual, everyday expression. You'll hear this spoken far more than written.

This meaning is used in publishing, editing, and typesetting. When a piece of text "runs in," it means it continues on the same line rather than starting a new paragraph or a new line.

Example:

  • "Run in the subheading with the paragraph below it."
  • "The editor asked for a run-in heading rather than a separate line."

Unless you work in publishing or design, you are unlikely to need this meaning in daily life — but it's worth knowing it exists so you aren't confused if you encounter it.
How to Tell the Meanings Apart

The context always makes it clear which meaning is being used. Here's a quick way to think about it:

Is it a noun? → It's almost certainly about a conflict or confrontation.
"He had a run-in with..." → disagreement or arrest-related trouble.

Is it a verb with a person as the object? → Likely about arrest.
"The police ran him in."

Is it a verb with a machine or vehicle? → About breaking in an engine.
"Running in the new engine."

Is it about entering a place briefly? → Literal/casual movement.
"I'll run in and grab it."

When "run-in" is a noun, it is hyphenated: a run-in.
When "run in" is a verb phrase, it is not hyphenated: she ran in quickly.

This is a standard English rule that applies to many phrasal verbs that double as nouns (think: "a break-in" vs. "they broke in").

As a noun (run-in):

  • A conflict or unpleasant encounter with someone
  • Specifically, trouble with police or the law

As a phrasal verb (run in / run someone in):

  • To arrest someone (police usage, British)
  • To drive a new engine carefully to let it settle (British)
  • To enter a place quickly and briefly

The most important meaning to master first is the noun sense — a run-in with someone — since it's the one you will encounter most often in books, news, conversations, and media. Once that's solid, the others follow naturally with a little practice.
14001:
To run something by someone means to tell someone about an idea, plan, or piece of information so that they can give their opinion, feedback, or approval.

In other words, you are sharing something with a person and giving them the chance to react to it — to say "yes, that's good," "no, that won't work," or "here's what I think."

Think of it this way: before you do something important, you want to check with someone you trust. You "run your idea by them" to see what they think.
Why These Words? Breaking It Down

Understanding why the words "run" and "by" are used together helps the meaning stick.

Imagine holding a piece of paper and quickly sliding it in front of someone's eyes so they can glance at it. You are literally running it by (= past) them — past their attention, past their eyes, past their judgment.

So "run something by someone" comes from the visual image of passing something in front of a person for them to review. Over time, this became a metaphor for sharing any idea, plan, or piece of information for someone's reaction or approval.

The structure is:

run + [something] + by + [someone]

The word "something" is the thing being shared (the idea, plan, proposal, news, etc.), and "someone" is the person whose opinion you want.

Here are the key grammar rules:

With a noun object, the noun goes between "run" and "by":

  • "Let me run this idea by you."
  • "She ran the plan by her manager."

With a pronoun object (it, this, that), the pronoun also goes between "run" and "by":

  • "Let me run it by you." ✅
  • "Let me run by you it." ❌ (This sounds unnatural and wrong.)

Tense changes follow the verb "run":

  • Present: "Let me run this by you."
  • Past: "She ran the idea by him yesterday."
  • Future: "I will run this by the team tomorrow."
  • Continuous: "I'm running something by my boss right now."
The Close Variation: "Run Something Past Someone"

There is one very common variation that means exactly the same thing:

"Run something past someone"

  • "Let me run this by you." = "Let me run this past you."

Both are equally correct and natural. "Past" replaces "by" and nothing else changes. You will hear both versions regularly, so it's important to recognize them as identical in meaning.

This idiom carries several subtle meanings beyond the surface definition:

1. You value the other person's judgment.
By saying "let me run this by you," you are signaling that you respect the other person enough to want their input. It is a polite and humble gesture.

2. You haven't fully committed yet.
Running something by someone usually happens before you take action. It suggests the matter is still open to change based on their feedback.

3. It can mean seeking approval OR just informing.
Sometimes you run something by someone because you need their approval (like a boss). Other times, you do it simply because you want a second opinion (like a friend). Context tells you which it is.

4. The tone is informal and conversational.
This is not a formal expression. You would say it to a colleague, friend, family member, or manager in casual settings. You would not write it in a formal legal document or official letter.

At work:

  • "Before I send this email to the client, let me run it by you."
  • "I have a new marketing idea — can I run it by the team in today's meeting?"
  • "She ran the budget proposal by the director before submitting it."

With friends or family:

  • "Hey, I have a plan for the weekend. Let me run it by you."
  • "I'm thinking of changing careers — I wanted to run it by you first."

Casual and short:

  • "Can I run something by you real quick?"
  • "I just want to run this by you before I decide."

When asking for repeated approval:

  • "I already ran the idea by my boss and she loved it."
A Special Use: "Run That by Me Again"

There is one slightly different but very common use of this idiom. When someone says "run that by me again," they are asking you to repeat or re-explain something — not because they want to approve it, but because they didn't fully understand or hear it the first time.

  • "Sorry, can you run that by me again? I got a bit lost."
  • "Run that by me one more time — what exactly are you proposing?"

In this specific use, the meaning shifts from "share this for my approval" to "say that once more so I can understand it better." Think of it as asking someone to pass the information by your ears or brain one more time.

To keep your understanding sharp, here is what "run something by someone" does not mean:

  • It does not mean to physically run while carrying something.
  • It does not mean to ignore someone's opinion — the whole point is to hear their reaction.
  • It does not mean you are obeying orders. You are inviting feedback, not taking instructions.
  • It is not the same as "run over something," which means to review or repeat something to yourself or a group (e.g., "let's run over the main points before the meeting").

If you ever need to express the same idea in more formal language, these phrases carry a similar meaning:

  • "I'd like to consult you on this."
  • "I'd like to get your input on this."
  • "I'd like to seek your feedback on this."
  • "I'd like to present this for your review."

But in everyday conversation, "run it by you" is far more natural and widely used.

"Run something by someone" = to share an idea or plan with someone in order to get their reaction, opinion, or approval before moving forward.

Once you understand that image — sliding something in front of someone's attention for them to look at — this idiom becomes very easy to remember and use naturally.
14002: A run-in describes an unwanted, unplanned meeting or clash with someone or something. The word carries a sense of friction — things bumping up against each other. Keep that idea of unplanned collision in mind; it ties most of the meanings together.
Meaning 1: A Conflict or Confrontation with a Person

This is by far the most common use of the word. A run-in is a brief but tense argument, quarrel, or unpleasant encounter with someone. It is usually unexpected, it is uncomfortable, and it is short. It doesn't mean a long, drawn-out fight — it's more like a sharp, sudden clash.

Examples:

  • "I had a run-in with my landlord about the broken heater."
    → I had an unpleasant exchange with my landlord. We clashed over the issue.
  • "She's been avoiding her colleague ever since their run-in last week."
    → They had some kind of confrontation or sharp disagreement.
  • "The two brothers had a run-in at the family dinner."
    → Things got heated and unpleasant between them.

Notice that a run-in doesn't have to be a screaming match. Even a cold, awkward, or tense exchange qualifies. The key is that something went wrong between two people — it was not a pleasant meeting.
Meaning 2: A Run-in with the Law (or Authority)

A very common, specific use of "run-in" is in the phrase "a run-in with the law." This means getting into trouble with the police or the legal system. More broadly, you can have a run-in with any authority figure — a school principal, a security guard, a government official.

Examples:

  • "He had a run-in with the law in his twenties but has stayed out of trouble since."
    → He was arrested or questioned by police at some point.
  • "The company had a run-in with tax authorities last year."
    → The company got into trouble with the tax department.
  • "She had a run-in with the school principal after skipping class."
    → She was called out and confronted by the principal.

This use follows the same logic as Meaning 1 — it's an unplanned, unwanted, unpleasant clash — only here, the other party is someone in a position of power over you.
Meaning 3: The Final Stretch Before Something (British English)

In British English especially, run-in is used to describe the final period or approach leading up to a major event. Think of it like a runner's final sprint toward the finish line — the last leg of the journey.

Examples:

  • "The run-in to the general election has been very dramatic."
    → The final weeks/days before the election.
  • "The team lost two players injured during the run-in to the championship."
    → During the final matches or stages of the season.
  • "Retailers always get very busy in the run-in to Christmas."
    → The weeks just before Christmas.

This meaning is quite different from the first two. There's no conflict here — just a sense of the closing approach to something important. You'll mostly hear this in British newspapers, sports commentary, or discussions about events (elections, seasons, holidays, deadlines).

In the world of publishing, design, and typography, a run-in refers to text that continues on the same line rather than starting on a new, separate line.

The clearest example is a run-in heading — a section heading or title that sits on the same line as the text that follows it, instead of standing alone on its own line above the paragraph.

Example — Run-in heading:

Health tips. Always drink enough water, eat balanced meals, and sleep for at least seven hours.

Here, "Health tips." is the heading, but instead of sitting on its own line, it runs directly into the paragraph. That's a run-in heading.

Compare it with a standalone heading:

Health tips.
Always drink enough water, eat balanced meals, and sleep for at least seven hours.

The term "run-in" can also apply to text in general — if a quote, sentence, or passage is absorbed into the flow of regular body text rather than displayed separately (like in a blockquote), it is said to be "run in."

You'll encounter this meaning if you work with writing, editing, design, or publishing.
Meaning 5: In Mechanics — The Break-in Period (Specialized)

In engineering and automotive contexts, a run-in (sometimes called a break-in) is the initial period of operating a new engine, machine, or mechanical device so that its parts can gradually settle, adjust, and smooth out against each other. During this period, the machine is usually operated gently and not pushed to its full capacity.

Examples:

  • "The manual says the engine needs a 500-mile run-in before you drive at high speeds."
  • "After the run-in period, the machinery performed much better."

The idea is that new mechanical parts have tiny rough edges that gradually wear smooth through careful initial use. The run-in period is when that happens.

You'll encounter this meaning in car manuals, engineering documents, or conversations about machinery.

In cricket, a run-in refers to the approach a bowler takes — the act of running toward the wicket before delivering the ball. It's the bowler's run-up.

This is a narrow, sport-specific use. If you're not interested in cricket, you can safely set this aside.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "run-in" has multiple meanings, context does all the work:

  • If someone is talking about people clashing, arguing, or getting into trouble → Meaning 1 or 2 (conflict/confrontation).
  • If someone mentions the law, police, or authority → almost certainly Meaning 2.
  • If someone is discussing a countdown to an event (an election, a sporting season, a holiday) → Meaning 3 (final stretch).
  • If the context is books, publishing, design, or document layout → Meaning 4 (typography).
  • If the context is engines, cars, or machines → Meaning 5 (break-in period).
  • If the context is cricket → Meaning 6.

MeaningIn one line
Conflict with a personA brief, tense, unpleasant clash with someone
Trouble with authorityGetting into conflict with police, law, or officials
Final stretch (British)The closing period before a major event
TypographyText or a heading that continues on the same line, not a separate one
MechanicsThe initial gentle-use period for a new engine or machine
CricketA bowler's approach run before delivering the ball

The meaning you will encounter in everyday life, by a wide margin, is the first one: a run-in = an unpleasant, brief clash with someone. Master that, and you've covered the word as most people use it. The rest are either British-English-specific, or confined to specialized fields.
14003:
When you call something run-of-the-mill, you are saying it is completely ordinary — nothing special, nothing bad, just average. It is the kind of thing that is so standard and typical that it leaves no impression on you. It doesn't surprise you. It doesn't disappoint you either. It simply exists, blends in, and is quickly forgotten.

Think of it this way: if you lined up a hundred examples of something, a run-of-the-mill version would be the one that perfectly represents the middle of the crowd — not the best, not the worst, just... there.

This is important: run-of-the-mill is not a neutral word. It carries a mild sense of disappointment or dismissal. When you use it, you are subtly suggesting that something could have been better, or that it failed to impress you. You aren't angry about it — you're just unexcited.

It is the verbal equivalent of a shrug.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "It was an ordinary meal." → Neutral. Just stating a fact.
  • "It was a run-of-the-mill meal." → Slightly dismissive. You expected more, or you're pointing out its lack of anything remarkable.

So while both mean "average," run-of-the-mill has a quiet "so what?" attitude buried inside it.

This adjective is flexible. You can use it to describe almost anything:

  • People: "He's a run-of-the-mill politician — makes big promises, delivers little."
  • Places: "It was a run-of-the-mill hotel — clean, functional, completely forgettable."
  • Things: "She bought a run-of-the-mill laptop — good enough for basic tasks, nothing remarkable."
  • Events: "The concert was run-of-the-mill. The band played well, but there was no energy, no magic."
  • Ideas or work: "The report was run-of-the-mill. It covered the basics but offered no new insights."
  • Experiences: "The movie was a run-of-the-mill thriller — predictable plot, predictable ending."

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. Run-of-the-mill does not mean terrible or broken. It means unremarkable. The hotel room was clean. The laptop works. The meal was edible. The performance was technically fine.

The criticism is not "this failed."
The criticism is "this never rose above the minimum."

If something is truly bad, you would use words like terrible, awful, or poor. Run-of-the-mill sits above that — it's the land of "fine," "okay," and "nothing to write home about."

It sits at a mild-to-moderate level of criticism on a scale. Here's a rough picture:

Extraordinary → Excellent → Good → Decent → Run-of-the-mill → Poor → Terrible

It lands just below "decent" — it's the point where you stop giving something credit for doing the bare minimum.

Run-of-the-mill is informal-to-neutral language. You can use it comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Casual writing (reviews, blogs, opinion pieces, emails)
  • Journalism and commentary

You would generally avoid it in highly formal or academic writing, where you'd prefer "unremarkable," "mediocre," or "undistinguished."
Words That Mean the Same Thing

These synonyms will help you fully grasp the word by seeing it from multiple angles. All of these share its core meaning but differ slightly in tone or emphasis:

  • Ordinary — the simplest, most neutral synonym
  • Average — emphasizes being mathematically in the middle
  • Mediocre — slightly stronger criticism; implies falling short of what was needed
  • Unremarkable — no feature worth noticing; very close in meaning
  • Commonplace — so typical it is everywhere
  • Pedestrian — dull and unimaginative (often used for writing or ideas)
  • Humdrum — repetitive and boring
  • Garden-variety — another informal phrase meaning plain and standard (e.g., "a garden-variety excuse")
  • Plain-vanilla — informal; meaning the most basic, unadorned version of something
  • Forgettable — emphasizes the lack of lasting impression

To understand a word fully, knowing its opposites is just as powerful:

  • Exceptional — far above average
  • Extraordinary — beyond what is ordinary
  • Outstanding — stands out clearly above the rest
  • Remarkable — worth noticing and talking about
  • Distinctive — has unique qualities that set it apart
  • One-of-a-kind — completely unique
  • Stellar — impressively excellent
  • Noteworthy — deserving attention

In real life, run-of-the-mill almost always appears right before a noun:

  • a run-of-the-mill experience
  • a run-of-the-mill student
  • a run-of-the-mill job
  • a run-of-the-mill story

You can also use it after a linking verb like "be":

  • "The presentation was run-of-the-mill."
  • "His work is run-of-the-mill at best."

The phrase "at best" is a very natural partner for this word, because it adds to the dismissive tone: "It was run-of-the-mill at best" means "Even the kindest thing I can say about it is that it was average."
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine you walk into an ice cream shop that claims to be the best in the city. You order a scoop, take a bite, and think: "This is just... ice cream. Cold, sweet, okay. I've had this a thousand times. Nothing new here."

That ice cream? Run-of-the-mill.

It delivered exactly what ice cream is supposed to deliver — no more, no less — and left you with zero excitement, zero memory, and zero reason to go back.

That feeling — completely average, quietly underwhelming, utterly forgettable — is what "run-of-the-mill" captures every time it is used.
14004:
"Run-of-the-mill" means ordinary, average, and nothing special. It describes something — or someone — that is completely standard, unremarkable, and does not stand out from the crowd in any way. There is nothing particularly good or bad about it; it is just… typical.

Think of it as the opposite of extraordinary. If something is run-of-the-mill, it won't impress you, won't surprise you, and won't disappoint you either. It simply exists in a forgettable, perfectly average zone.

This idiom has a fascinating and very literal history. It comes from the world of mills — specifically, textile mills and flour mills that were common in the 18th and 19th centuries in Britain and America.

In those days, a mill would produce large quantities of cloth or flour. Before this output was inspected, sorted, or graded for quality, it was called the "run of the mill" — meaning whatever the mill simply ran out as its basic, default production. It was the raw, unsorted, unexamined output.

The highest-quality pieces were separated and sold at a premium. The ordinary, ungraded material that required no special attention — the stuff that was just the standard product of the machine — was the "run of the mill."

Over time, this phrase moved out of factories and into everyday language. People began using it to describe anything that was just like that unsorted, unremarkable mill output: plain, standard, and without distinction.

"Run-of-the-mill" is an adjective phrase — meaning it describes nouns (people, things, events, places, ideas). It almost always comes before the noun it describes, though it can also come after a linking verb like is or was.

Notice the hyphens: when it comes before a noun, it is written with hyphens — run-of-the-mill. This is standard in English when multiple words work together as a single adjective before a noun.

Examples:

  • "It was a run-of-the-mill action movie — good for passing time, but nothing you'd remember a week later."
  • "He gave a run-of-the-mill performance. Technically correct, but completely uninspiring."
  • "The restaurant was run-of-the-mill — decent food, nothing worth recommending to a friend."
  • "I expected something extraordinary, but the interview turned out to be completely run-of-the-mill."
  • "She didn't want a run-of-the-mill career; she wanted to do something truly meaningful."
The Tone and Feeling Behind It

This phrase carries a mildly dismissive or underwhelmed tone. When you call something run-of-the-mill, you are not insulting it harshly — you are simply saying it failed to impress or distinguish itself. It is a soft criticism, or sometimes just a neutral observation.

If you say, "The hotel was run-of-the-mill," you are not saying it was terrible. You are saying it was completely forgettable — the kind of place you'd stay in without complaining, but also without ever telling anyone about it.

This is an important nuance: run-of-the-mill is not the same as bad. It is the absence of greatness, not the presence of failure.

Almost anything can be described this way:

  • A person: "He's a run-of-the-mill accountant — does his job, but brings no innovation."
  • An experience: "The concert was run-of-the-mill — just another evening out."
  • An idea: "The proposal was run-of-the-mill — nothing the team hadn't heard before."
  • A product: "It's a run-of-the-mill laptop — functional, but not exciting."
  • A day: "It was a run-of-the-mill Tuesday — nothing happened, nothing changed."

Knowing related words helps you feel the full range of this idiom's meaning:

  • Ordinary — the most direct synonym
  • Average — standard, in the middle of the range
  • Mediocre — slightly more negative; suggests it barely meets expectations
  • Unremarkable — nothing worth remarking on
  • Commonplace — so common it has become expected
  • Garden-variety — another idiom with the exact same meaning (also very common in everyday speech)
  • Nothing to write home about — an idiomatic phrase meaning the same thing
  • Dime-a-dozen — so common and ordinary that it has little value

Among these, mediocre is slightly harsher — it suggests something is barely good enough. "Run-of-the-mill," by contrast, is more neutral.

• Extraordinary — far beyond ordinary
  • Exceptional — standing out from the norm in a positive way
  • Outstanding — noticeably better than average
  • One-of-a-kind — unique; there is nothing else like it
  • Remarkable — worth remarking on because of how impressive it is

Do not use "run-of-the-mill" to describe something that is actively bad or genuinely terrible. That would be an overreach. If a movie was catastrophically bad, calling it "run-of-the-mill" would actually be a compliment by comparison. Use words like dreadful, poor, or terrible for truly bad things.

Reserve "run-of-the-mill" for things that are perfectly fine but completely unmemorable.
Register: When and Where Is It Used?

This is an informal, conversational idiom. You will hear it in everyday speech, see it in casual writing, journalism, and reviews. It is natural in spoken English and in emails or messages between friends and colleagues. It would feel slightly out of place in a formal academic paper or a legal document — in those contexts, you would simply write "ordinary" or "unremarkable."

Core meaningOrdinary, average, nothing special
OriginUnsorted, ungraded output from a textile or flour mill
Part of speechAdjective phrase
ToneMildly dismissive; neutral-to-slightly negative
RegisterInformal, everyday use
Closest synonymOrdinary / garden-variety

In a single sentence: if something is run-of-the-mill, it is as standard and unexciting as the plain, unsorted output of an old factory — it works, it exists, but it leaves no impression whatsoever.
14005: The word runaway as an adjective captures one central idea: something that has broken free from control and cannot easily be stopped. Think of a horse that has bolted — it's moving on its own, faster than anyone intended, and nobody can rein it in. That image is the heart of this word.
The Core Meaning: Out of Control

When you place "runaway" before a noun, you are saying that the thing described has gone beyond normal limits — it has "run away" from anyone's ability to manage or contain it.

Runaway inflation means prices are rising so fast and so relentlessly that the government cannot stop them. Nobody is in control anymore.

A runaway train is a train moving at dangerous speed with no one steering it. The brakes don't work. It just keeps going.

Runaway spending means money is being spent far faster than it should be, and nobody seems able to put the brakes on.

In all these cases, the thing has "escaped" from normal boundaries.

Because something "out of control" is also something happening at a scale far beyond the ordinary, "runaway" is also used to describe things that are hugely, almost shockingly successful or dominant — far beyond what anyone predicted.

A runaway success is not just a success. It is a massive, extraordinary success — one that exceeded every expectation and just kept growing. If a small film nobody expected to do well suddenly earns billions of dollars, people call it a runaway success.

A runaway victory means someone won by such a large margin that there was really no contest. They didn't just win — they dominated.

The idea here is still the same: the thing has gone so far beyond normal that it feels unstoppable.
Extended Meaning 2: Relating to a Person or Animal That Has Fled

"Runaway" can also describe a person or animal that has physically run away — left home, escaped, or bolted — especially when that act of fleeing is a defining feature of the situation.

A runaway teenager is a teenager who has left home without permission and cannot be found.

A runaway horse is a horse that has bolted, broken free from its rider or stable, and is galloping away uncontrolled.

A runaway bride is a bride who flees before or during her own wedding — she has "run away" from the commitment.

Notice how even here, the idea of being out of normal bounds is present: these people or animals have stepped outside the control or expectations of their situation.
Extended Meaning 3: Done Secretly, in Haste, as an Escape

Closely related to the above, "runaway" can describe something done by eloping or secretly fleeing, usually to escape restrictions.

A runaway marriage (or runaway wedding) is one where two people secretly run away together to get married, often because their families disapprove. The act itself is an escape.
The Single Thread That Connects All Meanings

No matter which sense you encounter, the adjective "runaway" always implies something has broken loose from normal limits — whether it's a physical escape, a process that is uncontrollable, or a result that far exceeds what was expected.

SituationWhat has "run away"?
Runaway inflationPrices have escaped from normal, manageable levels
Runaway successSuccess has escaped from ordinary expectations
Runaway teenagerA person has physically escaped from home
Runaway trainA vehicle has escaped from human control
How It Feels in a Sentence

Notice how the word signals drama and urgency. When you say "runaway," you are telling the listener: this thing is not just big or fast — it is beyond ordinary reckoning. It carries a sense of alarm, awe, or helplessness depending on context.

"The startup became a runaway hit overnight" — awe, excitement.

"Runaway debt is threatening the economy" — alarm, urgency.

"They caught a runaway suspect near the border" — the person fled and was difficult to contain.

Runaway (adjective) = out of control, unstoppable, or far beyond normal limits — whether describing a physical escape, a process nobody can halt, or something that has succeeded beyond all reasonable expectation. The word always carries the sense that something has "broken free" and is moving on its own terms, not anyone else's.
14006: A runaway is something or someone that has broken free from control and is now moving, acting, or existing outside the bounds of where it should be — often in a way that is hard or impossible to stop.
The Most Common Use: A Person

The most frequent meaning of runaway as a noun is a person — almost always a child or teenager — who has secretly left home without permission and without telling anyone where they are going.

This person hasn't just gone for a walk. They've made a deliberate choice to leave, usually because something at home has become unbearable — abuse, conflict, extreme unhappiness, or fear. They are now living on their own, without their family's knowledge or approval.

"The police found the runaway hiding in an abandoned building."

"The shelter downtown takes in runaways and helps connect them with social workers."

Notice that the word itself carries a quiet weight. When you hear "a runaway," you instinctively sense vulnerability and urgency. It is not a neutral word. It suggests someone in trouble, someone escaping from something painful, and often someone who is now in danger.

Historically, the word was also used for enslaved people who escaped to freedom — people who literally ran away from captivity. This older usage still lives in historical writing.
A Runaway Can Also Be an Animal

The second common use of runaway as a noun refers to an animal — typically a horse — that has broken free from its handler and is running out of control.

"The runaway galloped straight through the marketplace before anyone could stop it."

A horse is powerful. When one breaks loose and bolts, no one can simply grab it and make it stop. That sense of uncontrollable momentum is exactly what the word captures.
A Runaway Can Also Be a Vehicle

A runaway can also refer to a vehicle — a truck, a train, a cart — that is moving without anyone controlling it, usually because the brakes have failed or no one is at the wheel.

"Emergency crews worked to slow the runaway before it reached the crowded station."

This is the same underlying idea: something that was supposed to be under control has broken free and is now going wherever momentum takes it.
What All These Meanings Have in Common

No matter whether the runaway is a teenager, a horse, or a truck — the word always signals three things:

  1. Escape — it has left where it was supposed to be.
  2. Loss of control — no one is currently steering or stopping it.
  3. Urgency — the situation demands immediate attention.

This is what makes runaway such a vivid word. It doesn't just describe movement. It describes movement that has gone rogue.

As a noun, it follows normal rules:

  • One person: a runaway
  • Many people: runaways

"The city's shelters were overwhelmed by the number of runaways seeking help."

There is a difference between someone who runs away (the action) and someone who is a runaway (the identity or label).

  • "She ran away from home last Thursday." → This describes what she did.
  • "She is a runaway." → This describes who she now is — someone living outside the home, unaccounted for.

The noun runaway is the label given to someone once running away has become their situation, not just a momentary act.

A runaway (noun) is a person (especially a young person who has fled home), an animal, or a vehicle that has escaped from control and is now moving or existing in an uncontrolled, unsanctioned way — often urgently and dangerously. The word always carries the idea of something that broke free and cannot easily be brought back.
14007:
A rundown is a structured summary or overview of something — a clear, organized account of the main points, details, or facts about a topic, situation, or event.

Think of it this way: imagine you missed a long, two-hour meeting at work. You don't have time to read the full 20-page report of what happened. So you ask a colleague, "Can you give me a rundown of the meeting?" They then tell you the key things that were discussed — briefly, clearly, and in an organized way. That summary they give you? That is a rundown.

A rundown is not just any summary. It has a few important qualities baked into it:

  • It is organized. A rundown goes through things in a logical order — often point by point, or item by item. It doesn't jump around randomly.
  • It covers the essential information. It includes what you need to know, without burying you in unnecessary detail.
  • It is relatively brief relative to the full subject. A rundown is not an exhaustive deep dive — it's a smart, efficient overview.

So the word sits comfortably between a vague mention (too little) and an overwhelming full report (too much). A rundown is the sweet spot — enough to clearly understand something.

While the core idea stays the same, "rundown" gets used in two slightly different ways depending on context:

1. A quick overview (the lighter version)
Here, a rundown is a fast, high-level summary — just the highlights. You use this when you want the big picture fast.

"Before the game starts, the commentator gave a rundown of each player on the team."

"Let me give you a quick rundown of today's schedule."

2. A thorough breakdown (the more detailed version)
Here, a rundown is a more complete, systematic account that goes through everything carefully, piece by piece. It's still organized and efficient, but more comprehensive.

"The accountant gave us a rundown of all the expenses for the year."

"She prepared a detailed rundown of every step in the process."

The difference between these two is mostly signaled by the adjective placed before it — quick rundown vs. detailed rundown vs. full rundown. Without any adjective, context usually makes the intended depth clear.

In baseball, a rundown has a very specific, technical meaning. It refers to a play where a baserunner gets caught between two bases, and the fielders on both sides chase the runner back and forth, trying to tag them out before they can safely reach either base. It's essentially a trap. This play is also sometimes called a "pickle" in casual baseball talk, but rundown is the standard term.

This meaning is entirely separate from the "summary" meaning. Context (a sports conversation vs. a general conversation) will always make it clear which one is intended.

In everyday language, you will almost always see "rundown" used with a small set of very natural verb and adjective pairings. Getting familiar with these will help you use and recognize the word naturally:

Common verbs used with "rundown":

  • give a rundown
  • get a rundown
  • provide a rundown
  • need a rundown
  • do a rundown

Common adjectives used before "rundown":

  • a quick rundown
  • a brief rundown
  • a full rundown
  • a complete rundown
  • a detailed rundown
What Makes "Rundown" Different from Similar Words?

You might wonder how "rundown" differs from words like summary, overview, or recap. Here's the distinction:

  • A summary is a general word — it just means a shortened version of something.
  • An overview tends to be more formal and high-level, like a bird's-eye view.
  • A recap usually refers specifically to repeating what already happened — it looks backward.
  • A rundown implies going through things systematically — it feels more like a structured list or briefing being delivered to you. It has an active, organized, almost "item-by-item" feel to it.

If someone says "Let me give you a rundown," you instinctively expect them to go through the points in a clear, organized sequence — not just give you a vague description.
A Few More Examples in Real Life

• "Before the surgery, the doctor gave me a rundown of all the risks involved."
  • "The coach gave the team a full rundown of the opponent's strategy."
  • "Can someone give me a rundown of what I missed while I was on vacation?"
  • "The guide provided a rundown of the museum's most important exhibits."
  • "The financial report included a rundown of every department's spending."

The noun rundown means a clear, organized summary or breakdown of information — covering the key facts or details of something in an efficient and structured way. It can be brief or detailed depending on context. Outside of a baseball setting, if someone asks for "a rundown," they want you to walk them through the important points in an organized, easy-to-follow way.
14008: A rune is a single character — a letter — from an ancient writing system used by Germanic and Norse peoples of Northern and Western Europe, primarily from around the 2nd century CE onward. These characters together formed what are called runic alphabets, the most well-known of which is the Elder Futhark (a set of 24 characters).

Runes look nothing like the letters you are reading right now. They are angular — built almost entirely from straight lines and sharp diagonal strokes, with very few curves. This is not accidental. Runes were almost never written on paper or parchment. Instead, they were carved — into stone, wood, bone, metal, or antler. When you are cutting into a hard surface with a blade or chisel, curves are difficult and impractical. Straight lines are not. So the shapes of runes evolved to suit carving. This is why a runic inscription on a stone looks so different from, say, written Latin.
Runes as letters with names and meanings

This is where runes differ from ordinary letters in a fascinating way. Each rune was not just a sound or a letter — it also had its own name and its own meaning. For example, one rune was called Fehu, and it represented the "F" sound, but Fehu also meant "cattle" or "wealth." Another rune, Tiwaz, represented the sound "T" and was named after Tyr, a Norse god associated with justice and war.

So when someone in ancient times carved a rune, they were not simply spelling out a word the way you might type a letter. They were also invoking the symbolic weight of that rune's meaning. This dual nature — letter and symbol — is central to understanding what a rune is.

This is impossible to separate from the concept of a rune, because historically the two were inseparable.

Ancient Germanic and Norse peoples believed that runes were not merely invented by humans — they were considered sacred, discovered knowledge, gifts of cosmic power. Runes were thought to carry real, active power. Carving a rune into an object was not just labeling it; it was believed to imbue that object with something — protection, strength, a curse, a blessing.

This meant runes were used in rituals, in spells, inscribed on weapons to make them more powerful in battle, on amulets to protect the wearer, on grave markers to honor and perhaps guard the dead. They were written on objects to invoke luck, healing, or harm.

As a result, the word rune came to carry a second, broader meaning: a mysterious or magical symbol — any mark, character, or sign believed to hold hidden power. This usage is not purely metaphorical; it reflects how deeply magic and writing were intertwined in these cultures.

By extension, rune stones are small, flat stones (or tiles made of wood, clay, or other materials) each inscribed with a single runic character. A set typically contains all the characters of a runic alphabet.

These are used for divination — a practice of seeking guidance, insight, or answers about the future or present circumstances. The person consulting the runes might draw one or several stones at random, then interpret the meaning of whichever rune(s) appeared. Each rune, with its symbolic meaning, is read as a kind of message or indicator.

Rune stones in this sense are not about ancient writing at all — they are a tool for seeking hidden knowledge. This practice connects back to the idea of runes as magical and meaningful beyond mere letters.
How the word is used today

Today, the word rune is used in a few overlapping ways:

  1. In historical and linguistic contexts, a rune is simply one character from a runic alphabet. Scholars, historians, and linguists use it this way.
  2. In spiritual and New Age contexts, runes (usually rune stones) are used for divination and self-reflection, drawing on the old symbolic meanings of each character.
  3. In fantasy, literature, games, and popular culture, the word rune has been adopted very broadly to mean any magical symbol or inscription — often one that grants power, activates a spell, or holds supernatural energy. Video games, novels, and films use it this way constantly. Here, a "rune" might not resemble historical runic writing at all — it's simply a mark with mystical force.
  4. Poetically or figuratively, a rune can refer to any mysterious, arcane, or deeply meaningful mark or inscription — something that seems to hold a secret or hidden significance.

A rune is, at its most precise, a single character from an ancient Germanic or Norse writing system — but one where every character also carried a name, a symbolic meaning, and was believed to hold real power. That belief in power is what stretched the word outward: today it means not just those ancient letters, but any symbol considered mysterious, magical, or charged with hidden significance. When you see the word rune — in a history book, a fantasy novel, or a spiritual text — it always carries this combination: the idea of a mark that means something beyond its surface appearance, whether that's a sound, a concept, a force, or a secret.
14009:
A rung is one of the horizontal bars on a ladder — the individual steps you place your feet on when climbing up or down.

Picture a typical ladder leaning against a wall. It has two long vertical rails running up the sides. Connecting those two rails, from top to bottom, are a series of short horizontal bars spaced evenly apart. Each one of those bars is a rung. Together, they give you a surface to step on as you climb.

So if a ladder has ten steps, it has ten rungs. The word refers to a single one of those steps.

The word "rung" isn't limited to ladders. It also refers to the horizontal bars connecting the legs of a chair — the small crossbars near the bottom that brace the legs together and keep the chair sturdy. These are also called rungs. You might hear someone say, "The cat scratched the rungs of the chair."

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and frequently used.

Because a ladder has levels — with the bottom rung being the lowest and the top rung being the highest — people use "rung" as a metaphor to describe a level or position within any system, hierarchy, or scale.

Think of society, a company, or a career as an invisible ladder. Every step up that ladder is a rung.

Examples:

  • "She started at the bottom rung of the company and worked her way up to manager."
    → She started at the lowest level and rose higher.
  • "Being born into a wealthy family placed him on a higher rung of society."
    → He occupied a higher position or status in society.
  • "He's still on the lowest rung of his career."
    → He's still a beginner, at the starting level.
  • "Moving to a senior role was a big step up the ladder — she had climbed another rung."
    → She advanced one level higher.

The key idea here is levels — like steps you can move up or down. A rung is one specific level within that progression.

The plural of rung is simply rungs.

  • "Be careful — two of the ladder's rungs are broken."
  • "He has climbed many rungs to get where he is today."

ContextWhat "rung" means
  • On a ladder or chair: a single horizontal bar or crosspiece.
  • In life, society, or work: a single level or step in a system of ranks or positions.

The connecting thread between both meanings is the same: a rung is always one distinct step or level within something that has multiple levels stacked above and below it. Whether it's a physical ladder you climb with your feet, or an imaginary one representing your career or social status, a rung is always one specific position on that scale.
